A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, methods, benchmarks, and retained results. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation experiments on four SBI benchmarks and Hodgkin–Huxley inference using electrophysiological recordings, including posterior and predictive results.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds a Langevin step-size ablation and effective-sample-size diagnostics.

M1.justification: Defensive mixtures move from a future-work suggestion in v1 to a specified Route B extension in v2 Appendix B.1: a mixture proposal, a sampling procedure, and new importance weights and normalization. Section 7 also describes adapting Route A to distance-based losses through amortized loss estimation and offline MCMC. These extend the proposed procedures, although neither extension receives a reported empirical evaluation.

E1.justification: Both versions use Gaussian Mixture, Two Moons, SLCP, Lorenz–96, and the same Hodgkin–Huxley application with Allen Cell Types recordings. The added diagnostics use retained benchmarks without introducing a distinct data domain or task.

E2.justification: Figure 1 retains the same NLE and NRE comparators and Route A/B variants. The prior curves added to the Hodgkin–Huxley marginal plots are reference distributions, not newly evaluated inference methods.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a step-size sweep at beta = 0.9 and an nESS protocol using 2,000 importance samples with a 10,000-simulation training budget. Appendix A.1 also replaces v1's stated increasing geometric noise schedule with decreasing noise scales and scale-specific step sizes. This revises the reported specification without establishing that the retained benchmark experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds quantitative investigations of both routes' stability: a Gaussian Mixture Langevin step-size ablation in Appendix A.1 and temperature-dependent weight-degeneracy diagnostics across all four benchmarks in Appendix D. These substantially develop failure modes that v1 mainly discussed qualitatively.

E5.justification: The new nESS analysis reports means and interquartile ranges over 30 independent tasks, with percentile shading in Figure 5. V2 also newly states that Figure 1 averages over held-out tasks. This adds statistical reporting but does not establish increased replication of the original experiments; their curves still lack uncertainty bands.

E6.justification: Figure 1's benchmark results are unchanged. New Figure 4 reports C2ST of 0.58 at step-size scale 4e-4, versus 0.88 at 1e-1 and 0.85 at 1e-7. New Figure 5 shows nESS peaking near beta = 1 and declining away from it, especially for SLCP and Lorenz–96. These add diagnostic findings without revising the main benchmark comparisons.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds a defensive-weight definition, Proposition B.2, and its proof of bounded weights and finite variance for beta in [0, 1]. This supplies a new guarantee for the modified proposal beyond the retained original NRE-weight guarantee on [1/2, 1]. Remark B.3 explains why beta > 1 requires additional moment conditions.

C1.justification: The central claims of joint observation/temperature amortization, two training routes, and competitive approximation remain. Section 7 newly claims an extension to Gao et al.'s distance-based losses while explicitly limiting the established theory to power posteriors. Defensive reweighting also becomes a supplied construction rather than solely future work.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the broad description of low MMD and near-chance C2ST across benchmarks with a qualified competitive-performance interpretation. It limits off-manifold benefits to local score extrapolation, identifies Hodgkin–Huxley as a qualitative application rather than ground-truth recovery, and distinguishes weight degeneracy from posterior accuracy. These refine the existing limitations discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access link, explains held-out tasks and simulation-budget notation, and documents the Langevin step-size formula and diagnostic tuning procedure. However, Appendix A.1 drops v1's explicit T = 10, gamma_min = 0.01, and gamma_max = 1.0 settings. The changes improve some implementation guidance while removing other reproducibility details.

R1.justification: V2 newly positions its general-loss extension as building directly on Gao et al.'s amortized cost estimation. The broader related-work discussion remains stable. Updates to the Battaglia, Bishop, and Hyvärinen references concern the same cited works and do not constitute new literature coverage.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most exposition remain intact. V2 makes focused rewrites to results and limitations, expands protocol and sampler explanations, clarifies pseudocode indexing, and adds appendix subsections. Header, terminology, and bibliographic edits accompany these localized changes.

P2.justification: V2 adds the step-size and nESS figures, adds dashed prior curves to Figure 2, relocates the predictive panel, and changes typography and page flow to proceedings formatting. The main benchmark plot and existing appendix visualizations are retained; the latter become Figures 6–7.

improvement.justification: V2 better supports the routes' stability discussion through targeted diagnostics and a defensive-weight proof, and its interpretation of the unchanged benchmark results is more appropriately qualified. These gains are tempered by the absence of empirical evaluation of the defensive extension and the removal of explicit noise-grid settings. Overall, the paper becomes clearer and better substantiated without resolving its broader validation limitations.
